h1:
First Time in Trat
What to Know + a Plan
intro: Trat is the easternmost province in Thailand, with gorgeous water that sits further from Bangkok than most people expect. First-timers tend to get stuck on the same handful of questions: which island to pick, which pier to board, how much time to budget, and which month the sea actually runs clear. This guide pulls together everything you'll want to sort before you set off, then follows with a 3-day, 2-night plan that's already lined up the ferries and timing for you — so you're not left standing around or missing the last boat.

blocks.html: Before we get to the plan, here are the basics every first-timer in Trat should know — because Trat isn't the kind of beach town where you drive up and walk straight into the water. Most of the good stuff is out on the islands, which means a boat ride, and the distances are far enough that you really do need to plan your time.

blocks.text: How far is Trat, and how do you get there?

blocks.html: Trat town is around 300 km from Bangkok — about 4–5 hours by car, van or bus. If you're heading to an island, add the drive from town to the pier plus the boat crossing on top of that, so budget roughly half a day for day one. If you'd rather not drive, there are Bangkok–Trat flights into Trat Airport (near Laem Ngop) that cut the trip down to just over an hour — but flights are limited and prices swing depending on the season.

items: Driving yourself — the most flexible option. You can take the car straight onto the ferry and use it on the island, which is ideal if you want to hit several spots both in town and on the island.
Van or bus — from Ekkamai or Mo Chit into Trat town, then a songthaew (shared pickup) to the pier. Cheaper, but keep a close eye on the last departure times.
Flying — Bangkok–Trat is around 1 hour, landing at Trat Airport close to the pier. Good for short trips when you don't want the long drive.

blocks.title: You can do this without your own car
blocks.html: Take a bus into town, hop on a songthaew to the pier, then buy a walk-on passenger ferry ticket (no car needed). Once you're on the island, the red songthaews run along the beaches as a shuttle. The trade-off is that there are far fewer vehicles at night, so check the last run carefully.

blocks.text: Which island should you pick — Koh Chang, Koh Kood or Koh Mak?

blocks.html: This is the question first-timers ask most. Trat has three main islands with clearly different personalities. Don't try to cram several of them into one trip — you'll burn too much time on boats back and forth. Pick the one island that fits your style and do it properly.

items.name: Koh Chang
items.blurb: The biggest island in Trat and the easiest to get around, with plenty of beaches to choose from — lively White Sand Beach with everything you need, and quieter Klong Prao. You get both sea and waterfalls on one island, and it's only a 30–45 minute crossing from Laem Ngop. Great for a first visit.

items.name: Koh Kood
items.blurb: Thailand's fourth-largest island, with clear emerald water and a calm, quiet feel. Klong Chao Beach and Ao Tapao are stunning. Best if you genuinely want to switch off rather than party. It's a 1–1.5 hour speedboat ride from Laem Sok.

items.name: Koh Mak
items.blurb: A small, easygoing island you can loop around by bicycle or motorbike. The shallow water is fine for kids, and it makes a handy base for snorkelling at nearby Koh Rang. Great for families and anyone who likes a slow pace.

blocks.title: The short version, to make it easy
blocks.html: First visit, want easy access with both sea and waterfalls — go to Koh Chang · After quiet, clear water and proper rest — go to Koh Kood · Travelling as a family or just want laid-back snorkelling — Koh Mak is the best fit.

blocks.text: What to know about the ferry before you go

blocks.html: If you're heading to Koh Chang, the crossing is where people slip up most often — the ferry runs on set departures with a last boat, so it's not a case of pulling up to the pier and boarding any time. Knowing the timing in advance takes the guesswork out of day one.

items: The popular pier — Ao Thammachat ferry terminal (Khlong Yai subdistrict, Laem Ngop district), the fastest crossing at around 30–45 minutes.
Ferry times — first boat around 6:30 am, last boat around 6:30 pm; the schedule can shift with the weather.
Fares — roughly 90 THB per person each way, and about 200 THB each way for a four-wheel car.
Rainy season — some days the ferry may not run if the swell is heavy, so check the pier's page before you set off.

blocks.title: Leave extra time on long weekends
blocks.html: On long weekends the queue of cars for the ferry can get long, so head to the pier early and don't cut it close to the last boat — that way you're not left wondering whether you'll make it.

blocks.text: Which month gives you the clearest water?

blocks.html: Trat has distinct seasons. The clear-water, easy-swimming stretch runs November–April. The rainy season, May–October, brings heavier swell, some cancelled ferry days and murkier water — but it also means fewer people, cheaper rooms, and waterfalls like Klong Plu running fuller and prettier in the late rains. If clear water is what you're after, the dry season is by far the best value.

blocks.title: Best stretch for sunsets
blocks.html: The west side of Koh Chang — beaches like Kai Bae — faces the sunset perfectly. The clearest skies and best light run roughly November–February.

items: Return ferry — around 180 THB per person (add roughly 400 THB per car for the round trip).
Accommodation — mid-range guesthouses and resorts start around 600–900 THB/night, split between two if you travel as a pair.
Seafood meals — around 150–300 THB per person per meal; pricier on the island than over in Laem Ngop.
Waterfall entry / island songthaews — Klong Plu waterfall is 40 THB for Thai adults; songthaews run around 50–100 THB per trip.
On a budget, a 3-day, 2-night trip comes to roughly 3,000–4,500 THB per person (not counting fuel or flights from Bangkok).

blocks.html: This plan centres on Koh Chang because it's the easiest to reach and has the widest mix of things to do. You start at Laem Ngop, picking up dried-seafood souvenirs and lunch before crossing, then take your time over two full days on the island. No rushing.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Laem Ngop → ferry crossing → check in on Koh Chang

items.activity: Arrive in Laem Ngop town and wander the dried-seafood market
items.note: Laem Ngop is known for shrimp paste, fish sauce, dried shrimp and ngob (fishermen's hats). Prices at the source are lower than buying on the island, so pick things up on the way in and stash them in the boot rather than lugging them home on the last day.

items.activity: Stop at the Laem Ngop viewpoint and the old pier bridge
items.note: There's a lighthouse and the 'easternmost tip of the land' sign, with Koh Chang sitting across the water as a distant line of hills. It's a nice trip-opening photo spot that people usually just drive past.

items.activity: Waterfront seafood lunch in Laem Ngop
items.note: The seafood here is fresh because it's a fishing town. Order blue crab, prawns and shellfish at prices that aren't as steep as on the island, then drive to the pier once you're full.

items.activity: Drive to the Ao Thammachat ferry and cross to Koh Chang
items.note: You can take a car straight onto the ferry; without one, park on the Laem Ngop side and switch to a songthaew on the island. The crossing takes around 30–45 minutes.

items.activity: Check in around White Sand Beach or Klong Prao
items.note: White Sand Beach is the liveliest, with restaurants, bars and convenience stores all in one place, while Klong Prao is quieter and more private, with several larger resorts.

items.activity: Catch the sunset at Kai Bae viewpoint / Kai Bae Beach
items.note: The island's west side faces the evening light perfectly. Kai Bae viewpoint closes around 4:30 pm, but you can settle in on Kai Bae Beach and wait the light out comfortably.
Prices on the island run higher than in Laem Ngop, so check the per-kilo price board before you order to avoid surprises.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Klong Plu waterfall → a full day at the beach

items.activity: Breakfast, then head to Klong Plu waterfall
items.note: Klong Plu runs year-round and opens around 8:00 am–4:30 pm. Entry is 40 THB for Thai adults and 20 THB for children. Go early while it's still quiet and the water's a refreshing temperature.

items.activity: Short walk in to the falls, then a swim
items.note: It's about a 500-metre walk in on a path that isn't too steep — wear non-slip shoes. There's a pool up top you can get into, and it's fine to bring kids.

items.activity: Back for a long stretch at the beach
items.note: Late morning light is lovely for the sea. Pick the beach in front of your place or move to one you want to try, and make the most of the whole afternoon in the water.

items.activity: Relax with a Thai massage by the beach
items.note: White Sand Beach has plenty of beachfront massage spots. A massage to ease the aches before evening is the part of the trip a lot of people end up loving most.

items.activity: Stroll around White Sand Beach and find dinner
items.note: In the evening White Sand Beach buzzes, with restaurants, bars and street food to graze your way through. Easygoing atmosphere.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: One last beach morning → ferry back to the mainland

items.activity: One last swim / morning beach walk
items.note: Save the morning for a final dip before check-out — the early sun isn't harsh yet and the water's clear.

items.activity: Check out + a light lunch on the island
items.note: Leave enough time so you're not rushing for the last ferry, and you won't be left wondering whether you'll make it.

items.activity: Drive to the pier and take the ferry back to Laem Ngop
items.note: Allow for the car queue at the ferry on long weekends. Once you're back on the mainland you can drive home to Bangkok or carry on to Chanthaburi.

items.activity: Stop by Ban Nam Chiao community before heading home (if you have time)
items.note: A two-faith canalside community in Laem Ngop, with local food and crafts like the woven ngob hat. A nice place to round things off before the drive back.

blocks.title: What to pack
blocks.html: Sunscreen and non-slip shoes for the waterfall · any personal medication, since pharmacies are scarce on the island · spare cash, as some island spots don't take transfers · a power bank, in case a place loses power briefly during the rainy season.

faq.q: Which island should I pick for my first time in Trat?
faq.a: For a first visit, go with Koh Chang — it's the easiest to reach, just a 30–45 minute crossing from Laem Ngop, and it has both sea and waterfalls on one island. If you want somewhere very quiet with extra-clear water, head to Koh Kood; Koh Mak suits families and anyone who likes a relaxed, laid-back feel.

faq.q: How many days do I need for a first trip to Trat?
faq.a: If you're heading to an island, allow at least 3 days and 2 nights per island, since you lose time to the boat crossing both ways plus the 4–5 hour drive from Bangkok. If you're only doing the town and nearby communities, 1–2 days is enough.

faq.q: Which pier do I take to Koh Chang, and how much is it?
faq.a: The popular one is the Ao Thammachat ferry terminal in Laem Ngop district, with the fastest crossing at around 30–45 minutes. Fares are roughly 90 THB per person each way and about 200 THB each way for a four-wheel car. The first boat is around 6:30 am and the last around 6:30 pm.

faq.q: Which month has the clearest water in Trat?
faq.a: November–April is the clearest and best for swimming. The rainy season, May–October, brings heavier swell, some cancelled ferry days and murkier water — but it's also the quiet season with cheaper rooms and a fuller, prettier Klong Plu waterfall.

faq.q: Can I visit Trat without my own car?
faq.a: Yes. Take a van or bus from Bangkok into Trat town, switch to a songthaew to the Laem Ngop pier, then buy a walk-on passenger ferry ticket. On the island, the red songthaews run along the beaches as a shuttle — just keep a close eye on the last run, since there are far fewer vehicles at night.
